sentences.nl: Vandaag gaan Martin, Marieke en Gianluca, naar het café.
sentences.en: Today, Martin, Marieke, and Gianluca are going to the café.

sentences.en: They are going to watch football at the café.

sentences.nl: Ze staan op straat voor de flat van Martin.
sentences.en: They are standing on the street in front of Martin's apartment building.

sentences.en: "Is it far to the café?" Marieke asks.

sentences.nl: Hoe moeten we lopen? — Eerst lopen we rechtdoor.
sentences.en: How should we walk? — First, we walk straight ahead.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• How must we walk? — First walk we straight.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Hoe moeten we lopen?" uses inversion in questions where the verb "moeten" (must) comes before the subject "we" (we).  
• The word "eerst" (first) indicates sequence and is used at the beginning of the clause.  
• "Rechtdoor" means "straight ahead" and is an adverb indicating direction.

Examples:  
• "Wanneer gaan we eten?" (When are we going to eat?)  
• "Eerst eet ik ontbijt." (First, I eat breakfast.)  
• "We rijden rechtdoor." (We drive straight ahead.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Hoe laat moeten we vertrekken? — Eerst pakken we onze spullen in." (What time do we have to leave? — First, we pack our things.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Directions in the Netherlands are often given using simple terms like "rechtdoor" (straight ahead), "links" (left), and "rechts" (right) due to the well-organized urban planning with clear signages.

sentences.nl: Dan gaan we de tweede straat naar links.
sentences.en: Then we take the second street to the left.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Then go we the second street to left.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Dan" is an adverb meaning "then," indicating a sequence in actions.  
• "Gaan" is the verb "to go" in the present tense, first person plural.  
• "De tweede straat naar links" is a directional phrase; "de tweede straat" means "the second street," and "naar links" means "to the left."   
• Word order follows a typical structure where the verb comes after the time indication "Dan." 

• Examples:  
  - "Dan gaan we naar huis." (Then we go home.)  
  - "Daarna nemen we de bus naar het centrum." (Then we take the bus to the center.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Daarna lopen we de derde straat naar rechts." (After that, we walk the third street to the right.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)

sentences.nl: En dan meteen naar rechts.
sentences.en: And then immediately to the right.

sentences.nl: Het café zit op het einde van die straat.
sentences.en: The café is at the end of that street.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• The café sits at the end of that street.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Het café" is the subject, meaning "the café."  
• "Zit" is a form of "zitten" which can mean "sit" or "be located," used here to indicate location.  
• "Op het einde" means "at the end," with "op" as a preposition indicating location.  
• "Van die straat" translates to "of that street," with "van" showing possession or association.  
• Example phrases:  
  - "De winkel ligt op de hoek van de straat." (The store is located on the corner of the street.)  
  - "Het huis staat aan het begin van de laan." (The house is at the beginning of the avenue.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Het restaurant zit naast de supermarkt. (The restaurant is next to the supermarket.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, cafés are not just places for coffee; they often serve alcohol and light meals, functioning more like pubs or bars.

sentences.nl: Daar is het café.
sentences.en: There is the café.

sentences.nl: In het café is het niet druk.
sentences.en: It is not busy in the café.

sentences.nl: ‘Het is hier rustig’, zegt Marieke.
sentences.en: "It is quiet here," says Marieke.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• "It is here calm," says Marieke.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The sentence has a subject-verb-object (SVO) order: "Het is hier rustig" ("It is here calm").  
• The verb "is" is in the present tense, indicating a current state.  
• The adjective "rustig" follows "hier," describing the state of the location.

• Example: "Het is daar druk." (It is busy there.)  
• Example: "Het is nu warm." (It is warm now.)  
• Example: "Het is altijd gezellig." (It is always cozy.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Het is overal stil," zegt Pieter. (It is quiet everywhere, says Pieter.)

sentences.nl: ‘Hmmm …’, zegt Martin.
sentences.en: "Hmmm ...," says Martin.

sentences.nl: Normaal zijn hier altijd veel mensen.
sentences.en: Normally, there are always many people here.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Normally are here always many people.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Normaal" is an adverb meaning "normally" or "usually".  
• "Zijn" is the verb "to be" in the present tense.  
• "Hier" means "here", indicating location.  
• "Altijd" means "always", emphasizing frequency.  
• "Veel mensen" means "many people", where "veel" is used to describe a large quantity.

- Er zijn normaal gesproken veel katten in de tuin. (There are usually many cats in the garden.)
- Op zaterdagen zijn hier altijd veel kinderen. (On Saturdays, there are always many children here.)
- Normaal doet hij dat niet. (Normally, he doesn't do that.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Normaal regent het hier elke dag. (Normally, it rains here every day.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In many Dutch cities, particularly in popular tourist areas or city centers, it is common to see a lot of people. The sentence might reflect an observation about a busy place that is unusually quiet.

sentences.nl: Vooral bij een voetbalwedstrijd.
sentences.en: Especially at a football match.

sentences.nl: Wanneer begint de wedstrijd? — Om 9 uur.
sentences.en: When does the match start? — At 9 o'clock.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Wanneer begint de wedstrijd? — Om 9 uur.  
(When begins the match? — At 9 o'clock.)

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Wanneer" is a question word meaning "when."  
• "Begint" is the present tense of "beginnen" (to begin/start), following normal verb-second order in questions.  
• "De wedstrijd" means "the match" or "the game."  
• "Om" is a preposition used for time, meaning "at."  
• "Uur" means "hour" or "o'clock," often used with numbers for time.

Extra phrases:  
– Wanneer komt de trein aan? (When does the train arrive?)  
– De film begint om 8 uur. (The movie starts at 8 o'clock.)  
– Om hoe laat vertrekt het vliegtuig? (At what time does the plane depart?)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Wanneer gaat de winkel open? — Om 10 uur. (When does the store open? — At 10 o'clock.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, punctuality is highly valued, and it's common to specify exact times for meetings and events.

sentences.nl: De achtste finale van de Champions League.
sentences.en: The Round of 16 of the Champions League.

sentences.nl: Welke clubs spelen tegen elkaar? — Ajax speelt thuis tegen AC Milaan.
sentences.en: Which clubs are playing against each other? — Ajax is playing at home against AC Milan.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Which clubs play against each other? — Ajax plays at home against AC Milan.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The sentence "Welke clubs spelen tegen elkaar?" uses "welke" (which) as an interrogative pronoun to ask questions about a specific group. "Tegen elkaar" means "against each other," often used in competitive contexts.  
• "Speelt thuis tegen" means "plays at home against," where "thuis" (at home) indicates the location.  
• Example: "Welke boeken lees jij?" (Which books do you read?)  
• Example: "Hij speelt vaak tegen zijn broer." (He often plays against his brother.)  
• Example: "Ze eet thuis." (She eats at home.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Welke teams strijden om de beker?" (Which teams are competing for the cup?)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Ajax is a famous football club in the Netherlands with a rich history, and matches against international teams like AC Milan are significant events for fans.

sentences.nl: Aha… dan zit iedereen natuurlijk in het stadion!
sentences.en: Aha... then everyone is of course in the stadium!
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Aha… then sits everyone of course in the stadium!

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "dan zit iedereen" uses "dan" which means "then," indicating a sequence or consequence.  
• "zit iedereen" uses "zit" (sits) in an informal way to mean "is located" or "is present."  
• "natuurlijk" means "of course," often used to express that something is expected or obvious.

- Iedereen zit in de tuin. (Everyone is in the garden.)  
- Natuurlijk regent het weer. (Of course, it is raining again.)  
- Dan ga ik naar huis. (Then I go home.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Aha… dan is het café natuurlijk vol! (Aha… then the café is of course full!)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, going to a stadium for sports events, especially football matches, is a common social activity and often involves a collective experience.

sentences.nl: Dat is hier toch vlakbij? — ‘Ja’, zegt Martin.
sentences.en: That's nearby, right? — 'Yes,' says Martin.

sentences.nl: Dat is 10 minuutjes fietsen.
sentences.en: That's a 10-minute bike ride.

sentences.nl: ‘Voor wie ben jij?’, vraagt Marieke aan Martin.
sentences.en: "Who are you for?" Marieke asks Martin.

sentences.nl: Voor Ajax natuurlijk!
sentences.en: For Ajax, of course!

sentences.nl: En voor wie ben jij? — Ook voor Ajax.
sentences.en: And who are you for? — Also for Ajax.

sentences.nl: Ook voor Ajax? — Jij komt toch uit Milaan? — Ja, ik kom uit Milaan,, maar ik ben een supporter van Inter!
sentences.en: Also for Ajax? — You are from Milan, right? — Yes, I am from Milan, but I am a supporter of Inter!
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Also for Ajax? — You come still from Milan? — Yes, I come from Milan, but I am a supporter of Inter!

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Word Order**: "Jij komt toch uit Milaan?" uses an inverted word order typical for questions, with "kom" (come) before the subject "jij" (you).  
• **"toch"**: This word is used for emphasis or to express surprise/confirmation, akin to "still" or "aren't you" in English.  
• **Prepositions**: "uit" here means "from," indicating origin.  
• **Example 1**: "Je woont toch in Amsterdam?" (You live in Amsterdam, don't you?)  
• **Example 2**: "Hij is toch je broer?" (He is your brother, right?)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Zij houdt toch van voetbal?" (She loves football, doesn't she?)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Ajax and Inter Milan are both famous football clubs, with Ajax being based in Amsterdam and Inter Milan in Milan. Supporting a team from another city is common and reflects the global nature of football fandom.

sentences.nl: En daarom ben ik altijd tegen AC Milaan.
sentences.en: And that's why I am always against AC Milan.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• And therefore am I always against AC Milan.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "En daarom" means "And therefore," showing cause and effect.  
• "ben ik" is the inversion of "ik ben" which occurs because "daarom" pushes the subject "ik" after the verb.  
• "tegen" means "against," used here to indicate opposition to something.

  - "Hij is tegen het plan." (He is against the plan.)
  - "Daarom ga ik niet." (Therefore, I am not going.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• En daarom eet ik nooit pindakaas. (And therefore, I never eat peanut butter.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• AC Milan is a prominent football club in Italy. In the Netherlands, football is a significant part of culture, and rivalries between clubs can be intense. Dutch fans may support or oppose international teams based on historical matches or player transfers.

sentences.nl: En jij Marieke? — Ik ben voor AC Milaan!
sentences.en: And you, Marieke? — I support AC Milan!

sentences.nl: Huh? — Maar Ajax is toch een Nederlandse club? — Ja, maar ik kom uit Rotterdam.
sentences.en: Huh? — But Ajax is a Dutch club, right? — Yes, but I come from Rotterdam.

sentences.nl: Ik ben voor Feijenoord.
sentences.en: I support Feyenoord.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• I am for Feyenoord.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Ik ben voor" translates to "I am for," indicating support or preference. "Voor" is a preposition used here to denote support.  
• "Feijenoord" is a Dutch football club name, often spelled as "Feyenoord."  
• Dutch sentences often follow the subject-verb-object order, but prepositions like "voor" can modify the object.  

Extra Examples:  
- "Ik ben voor Ajax." (I am for Ajax.)  
- "Zij is voorstander van verandering." (She is a proponent of change.)  
- "Wij zijn tegen geweld." (We are against violence.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Ik ben voor democratie." (I am for democracy.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Feyenoord is one of the major football clubs in the Netherlands, based in Rotterdam. Supporting a particular football club can be an important part of Dutch social identity and community.

sentences.nl: En dus ben ik tegen Ajax!
sentences.en: And so I am against Ajax!

sentences.nl: Nou Marieke, dat vind ik niet leuk!
sentences.en: Well Marieke, I don't like that!

sentences.nl: Tsja… vrouwen en voetbal…, dat gaat niet samen Martin…
sentences.en: Well... women and football..., that doesn't go together, Martin...
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Well... women and football..., that does not go together Martin...

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Dat gaat niet samen" is a phrase indicating that two things do not fit or work well together. "Samen" means "together," and "gaat" is the third person singular form of "gaan" (to go).  
• The ellipses "…" are used for pauses or to indicate continuation of thought, a common stylistic choice in informal writing or speech.  
• "Tsja" is an informal interjection similar to "well" or "um" used to express hesitation or contemplation.  

Extra examples:  
• "Koffie en slapen, dat gaat niet samen." (Coffee and sleeping, that does not go together.)  
• "Honden en katten, dat gaat soms niet samen." (Dogs and cats, that sometimes don't go together.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Kinderen en stilte, dat gaat niet samen." (Children and silence, that does not go together.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, as in many countries, football (soccer) is a popular sport, and the interplay between gender perceptions and sports can be a topic of casual conversation or humor.

sentences.nl: Hmmm ?!?!
sentences.en: Hmmm ?!?!

sentences.nl: Oeps, het is niet meer zo gezellig.
sentences.en: Oops, it is not so pleasant anymore.

sentences.nl: Martin is boos op Marieke.
sentences.en: Martin is angry with Marieke.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Martin is angry at Marieke.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Boos" is an adjective meaning "angry," and it is used with the preposition "op" to indicate who someone is angry at.  
• "Is" is the third person singular present tense form of "zijn" (to be).  
• Word order follows a simple subject-verb-object pattern here.

• Examples:  
  - "Zij is boos op haar vriend." (She is angry at her boyfriend.)  
  - "Wij zijn boos op de regering." (We are angry at the government.)  
  - "De leraar is boos op de klas." (The teacher is angry at the class.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Anna is blij met haar nieuwe baan." (Anna is happy with her new job.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)

sentences.nl: En Marieke is boos op Gianluca.
sentences.en: And Marieke is angry at Gianluca.

sentences.en: How does that continue? — We'll see that next time on ‘Heb je zin?’.

welke.spelling: The 'w' in Dutch is pronounced closer to an English 'v', while 'e' is short, creating /ɛ/.
welke.fast: The initial /ʋ/ in ‘welke’ may be pronounced as a [v] when followed by a vowel in fast speech.

dat.fast: In connected speech, the /d/ in ‘dat is’ may be voiced to a soft [d̪] before the vowel.
